subsystems.name: Nucleon-scale driver
subsystems.role: the hypothetical tool that would alter the internal state of atomic nuclei.

subsystems.name: Isomer and excited-state control
subsystems.role: putting nuclei into long-lived excited states and releasing that energy on demand.

subsystems.name: Containment and heat removal
subsystems.role: handling mega-electronvolt gamma and neutron fluxes without melting or irradiating the surroundings.

subsystems.name: Energy conversion
subsystems.role: turning nuclear excitation into electricity rather than waste heat.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics and feedback
subsystems.role: measuring what the nuclei are actually doing, in real time.

buildSteps.title: Choose an isotope
buildSteps.detail: Only a few nuclei have long-lived excited states with useful energy; the material must first be produced in a reactor or accelerator and separated.

buildSteps.title: Populate the excited state
buildSteps.detail: Nuclei are driven into a metastable state using particle beams or resonant gamma rays — an inherently inefficient, energy-hungry step.

buildSteps.title: Stabilise and store it
buildSteps.detail: The material has to sit in a dense, cold, shielded form without spontaneously releasing its stored energy; density and triggering sensitivity work against each other.

buildSteps.title: Trigger release
buildSteps.detail: A photon pulse at exactly the right energy would start the cascade. This is the step no experiment has yet demonstrated convincingly.

buildSteps.title: Capture the output
buildSteps.detail: The released gamma rays are absorbed in a surrounding mass and their heat carried away, or converted directly — a capability that does not exist at useful efficiency today.

buildSteps.title: Build the radiation barrier
buildSteps.detail: A "perfect shield" would mean nuclei that absorb or down-convert incoming radiation; in practice this reduces to very dense high-Z and hydrogen-rich layers, not nucleon engineering.

buildSteps.title: Contain and recycle
buildSteps.detail: Extreme induced radioactivity means the whole assembly must be handled remotely and the isotope inventory continuously replenished.

prerequisites.why: resonant nuclear excitation needs photons matched to nuclear transitions; sources exist but are large and inefficient.
long-lived isomers are real and well studied, but reliable on-demand triggering has never been reproduced.
storing nuclear excitation at useful density risks self-triggering and meltdown.

prerequisites.tech: Remote handling of intense induced radioactivity
prerequisites.why: mature in nuclear facilities, but not at the scale such a material would demand.
there is no efficient, scalable way to turn megaelectronvolt photons straight into current.

pathway.milestone: laboratory study of nuclear isomers and resonant excitation
pathway.unlocks: knowledge of which states exist and how hard they are to trigger. A widely reported late-1990s claim that a hafnium isomer could be triggered with low-energy X-rays was not reproduced by other laboratories.

pathway.milestone: compact, tunable gamma-ray sources such as gamma-ray free-electron laser concepts
pathway.unlocks: the ability to test triggering and storage on a bench rather than at a national facility.

pathway.milestone: reproducible energy release from a stored nuclear state
pathway.unlocks: the first evidence that any of this could be engineered rather than only theorised.

pathway.milestone: a closed, remotely handled energy-storage or shielding system
pathway.unlocks: nothing near-term; "perfect shielding" in the sense claimed here has no known physical mechanism, since no material can negate the radiation field around it.
